source.author: Al Brooks
source.chapter_title: Wedges and Other Three-Push Reversal Patterns

conventions: stop entries mechanized as signal-bar-close then next-bar-open; every tunable constant is a parameter; long side only in pseudocode (bear mirror per Brooks). swingHigh(n)/swingLow(n) = the n-th most recent confirmed swing pivot counting back from the current bar (1 = most recent), per the T17-01 pivotStrength-bar confirmation definition already established in the Trends book (a swing low at bar i needs pivotStrength lower bars on each side before it is confirmed, so it is only known pivotStrength bars after it forms). pushCount(direction, pivotStrength) = number of consecutive alternating-or-same-direction swing pivots extending the pattern in the stated direction.

candidates.name: ThreePushPatternPrimitive
candidates.quote: When the market makes three pushes in one direction and then creates a reversal setup that triggers the reversal trade... It does not matter if it is a wedge, a micro wedge, a parabolic wedge, a wedge with a fourth push... another type of triangle (including an expanding triangle), a triple top or bottom, a double top or bottom pullback, a head and shoulders top or bottom, or a failed breakout below a double top or above a double bottom.
candidates.description: Primitive: the market has made at least three sequential swing pushes in one direction (extreme, pullback, more-extreme, pullback, more-extreme). Brooks treats every three-push shape (wedge, triangle, expanding triangle, double/triple top or bottom, head and shoulders, failed breakout of a double top/bottom) as behaviorally the same setup regardless of whether the connecting lines converge, run parallel, or diverge.
candidates.book_order_type: n/a (pattern classification used as a precondition for other candidates in this file)

complexity.reason: needs swing-pivot detection (T17-01's pivotStrength-bar confirmation) plus a running count of successive same-direction pivots across a variable-length window; the shape test (converging/parallel/diverging lines) is explicitly NOT required by Brooks to trade it, so it is left out of this primitive

notes: Same underlying primitive as ThreePushWedgePattern (VP1-16), ThreePushesWedgePattern (V01-04), and ThreePushWedgePattern (R18-01 in the Ranges book); defined independently per chapter per convention, dedup pass should merge all four.
This is the chapter's core shared primitive; every other candidate below either depends on it or refines one of its named sub-shapes.

candidates.name: WedgeReversalMeasuredMoveTargets
candidates.quote: the first target is a test of the bottom of the wedge (the bottom of the pullback from the first push up), and the next is a measured move down, based on the height from the bottom to the top of the wedge.
candidates.description: After a successful reversal out of a wedge/three-push top, take partial profit at a test of the wedge's own starting extreme, and the balance at a measured move beyond that equal to the wedge's own height. Long-side mirror: reversal out of a wedge bottom targets a test of the wedge top, then a measured move up by the wedge height.
candidates.book_order_type: limit exit (or discretionary scale-out) at each target price

complexity.reason: wedgeTopPrice/wedgeBottomPrice are the pattern's own pivot extremes, so this inherits V05-01's swing-pivot detection before the arithmetic (itself trivial) can run

notes: Generic pattern-height measured move; recurs across many chapters as a shared primitive once pivot detection exists (see R18-08's leg1=leg2 variant).

candidates.name: FailedWedgeContinuationMeasuredMove
candidates.quote: If a wedge triggers an entry, but then it fails and the market extends one or more ticks beyond the wedge extreme, it will often run quickly to a measured move based on the height of the wedge.
candidates.description: If a wedge-reversal entry fails (price extends beyond the wedge's own extreme instead of reversing), the failure trade in the ORIGINAL trend direction targets a measured move equal to the wedge's own height, added beyond the wedge's far extreme.
candidates.book_order_type: limit exit (or discretionary scale-out) at the continuation target

complexity.reason: requires the same pivot-based wedge boundaries as V05-02 plus a failure test against the extreme

notes: Same target arithmetic as V05-02, applied in the opposite (with-trend continuation) direction once the reversal attempt fails.

candidates.name: WedgePullbackFirstSignalEntry
candidates.quote: Wedge pullbacks are discussed in Chapters 18 and 19 in the second book. When they are pullbacks in trends, they are with-trend setups and it is reasonable to enter on the first signal.
candidates.description: When a three-push pattern forms as a with-trend pullback (a wedge flag), enter with-trend on the first reversal signal bar once the pattern completes, without waiting for a second entry.
candidates.pseudocode:
isWedgePullbackSignal = isThreePushPattern(DOWN, pivotStrength)[1] && close[0] > open[0] && close[0] > high[1];
enterLongNextBarOpen = isWedgePullbackSignal
candidates.book_order_type: buy stop one tick above the signal bar's high

complexity.reason: inherits V05-01's pivot/leg-count detection plus needs an established-trend context filter defined elsewhere in the corpus

notes: Duplicate of WedgePullbackWithTrendEntry (R18-02) in the Ranges book, restated here verbatim by cross-reference ('discussed in Chapters 18 and 19').

candidates.name: WedgeReversalWaitForSecondEntry
candidates.quote: It is important to remember that a wedge reversal is a countertrend setup. It is therefore usually better to wait for a second entry, like a lower high... after a wedge top or a higher low... after a wedge bottom.
candidates.description: When a three-push pattern is acting as a countertrend reversal (not a with-trend pullback), skip the first breakout signal and wait for a second entry (a lower high / higher low pullback from the initial reversal attempt) unless the pattern is exceptionally strong.
candidates.book_order_type: n/a (gates whether to act on the first vs second reversal signal)

complexity.reason: 'exceptionally strong' is a discretionary judgment call with no stated bar-level test; a design decision (e.g., trend-bar count, overlap, body fraction) is needed before this can be coded

notes: Duplicate of WedgeReversalSecondEntryFilter (R18-03) in the Ranges book.

candidates.name: WedgeReversalMinDurationAndChannelLine
candidates.quote: A reversal usually needs to be at least 20 bars long and have a clear trend channel line to be strong enough to reverse a trend.
candidates.description: A three-push pattern acting as a trend reversal (as opposed to a with-trend flag) is only considered strong enough to reverse the trend if it has lasted at least N bars and has a clear trend channel line drawn across its pushes.

complexity.reason: requires trend-channel-line projection from pivots plus a persistent bar counter from the pattern's identified start

notes: Duplicate of ReversalPatternMinDurationFilter (R18-05) in the Ranges book, restated verbatim.
'Clear trend channel line' has no numeric definition; minChannelFitQuality is a placeholder for whatever line-fit quality measure the authoring pass adopts.

candidates.name: WedgeFlagDurationRange
candidates.quote: wedge flags are usually smaller patterns, and most last about 10 to 20 bars.
candidates.description: A with-trend wedge flag is typically 10 to 20 bars long from its first push to its completion; treat wedges outside this range as less typical.
candidates.pseudocode:
wedgeDurationBars = currentBarIndex - wedgeStartBarIndex;
isTypicalWedgeFlagLength = wedgeDurationBars >= minWedgeBars && wedgeDurationBars <= maxWedgeBars

complexity.reason: needs a persistent counter from the wedge's identified start bar (itself dependent on V05-01's pivot detection), but the count/compare itself is simple cross-bar state

notes: Duplicate of WedgeFlagDurationFilter (R18-04) in the Ranges book.

candidates.name: ParabolicWedgeAcceleration
candidates.quote: if there is a bull wedge and the slope of the trend channel line drawn across the tops of the second and third legs is steeper than the line drawn across the highs of the first two legs, the wedge is parabolic... if the market reverses down, it will usually do so in about two legs and 10 bars.
candidates.description: A wedge is parabolic when the trend-channel-line slope across its later two legs is steeper than the slope across its earlier two legs. A parabolic wedge is more climactic: expect the reversal, if it comes, to complete in about two legs and roughly N bars.
candidates.pseudocode:
lateSlope = slopeOfLine(swingHigh(1), swingHigh(2)); // pivots of legs 2 and 3
earlySlope = slopeOfLine(swingHigh(2), swingHigh(3)); // pivots of legs 1 and 2
isParabolicWedge = lateSlope > earlySlope; // for a bull wedge top; bear wedge bottom mirrors on lows
expectedReversalLegs = 2;
expectedReversalBars = 10
candidates.book_order_type: n/a (climax classification feeding the reversal expectation)

complexity.reason: needs swing-pivot detection plus a trend-line slope computed and compared across two overlapping three-pivot windows

notes: The 2-legs/10-bars figure is a general climax-correction expectation that likely recurs; check the corpus for an existing 'consecutive climax correction' primitive (e.g. VP1-20) before authoring.

candidates.name: ShrinkingStairsWedge
candidates.quote: When there are three or more pushes and each breakout is smaller, then this is a shrinking stairs pattern... It is a sign of waning momentum and increases the odds that there will be a two-legged reversal.
candidates.description: In a three-push pattern, if each successive push extends less far beyond the prior push than the one before it did (shrinking breakout increments), momentum is waning and the odds of a two-legged reversal increase.
candidates.pseudocode:
increment2 = swingHigh(1) - swingHigh(2); // third push beyond second
increment1 = swingHigh(2) - swingHigh(3); // second push beyond first
isShrinkingStairs = increment2 < increment1 && increment2 > 0 && increment1 > 0
candidates.book_order_type: n/a (momentum-fade classification feeding the reversal setup)

complexity.reason: needs swing-pivot detection to locate each push's extreme before the breakout increments can be differenced

notes: No numeric threshold given for the increment shrinkage; a strict less-than comparison is Brooks's own description ('smaller than the prior one').

candidates.name: AvoidWedgeReversalInTightChannel
candidates.quote: If the channel is tight, even if it has a wedge shape, it is almost always better not to enter on the reversal. Instead, wait for the reversal and see how strong the breakout is.
candidates.description: If the channel containing the three-push pattern is tight (small pullbacks between pushes, high bar-to-bar overlap), skip the reversal entry entirely and wait to assess the strength of any subsequent breakout instead.
candidates.book_order_type: n/a (context filter that suppresses the reversal entry)

complexity.reason: 'tight channel' is used repeatedly in this chapter but never reduced to a numeric bar-level test; a design decision (overlap fraction, pullback-to-ATR ratio, or trend-bar fraction) is needed before this can be coded

notes: Recurs at least three times in this chapter (pp. 183, 194, 205) as the single most repeated qualifier for skipping a wedge reversal.

candidates.name: MicroWedgePattern
candidates.quote: A micro wedge is a wedge that is formed by three consecutive bars or three out of four or five consecutive bars.
candidates.description: A micro wedge is the same three-push pattern as V05-01 but confirmed with a minimal pivot-strength (adjacent-bar) pivot definition, so it can complete within three to five consecutive bars instead of the usual multi-bar swing pattern. Being so small, it usually produces only a minor correction.
candidates.book_order_type: n/a (pattern classification; traded like V05-01 but on a smaller scale)

complexity.reason: same swing-pivot mechanics as V05-01 with a smaller pivotStrength parameter; still requires pivot detection, not a fixed-offset bar test

notes: Effectively V05-01 with pivotStrength=1 and a tight max-duration cap.

candidates.name: MinorSwingOneTickBreakoutThreePush
candidates.quote: if the market is in a trading range and then has a one-tick breakout beyond a minor swing high or low that reverses for maybe three to 20 bars, and then the market again has another one-tick or sometimes a two-tick breakout that once again pulls back, those three pushes set up the pattern. If the market then breaks again beyond that second minor breakout, it usually leads to a significant breakout.
candidates.description: A minor swing extreme is broken by only one or two ticks, twice in succession, each time followed by a multi-bar pullback (3 to 20 bars); if price then breaks beyond the second minor breakout as well, treat it as a significant continuation breakout rather than a reversal, with a measured-move target equal to the pattern's height.
candidates.book_order_type: buy stop above the second minor breakout's extreme

complexity.reason: needs swing-pivot detection at a fine (one-to-two-tick) resolution plus a pullback-length window (3-20 bars) between each breakout

notes: This is a wedge that FAILS to reverse rather than one that succeeds; the trade is with the breakout, not against it.

candidates.name: FailedDoubleTopBreakoutActsAsWedgeTop
candidates.quote: if there is a double top and then the market breaks above the double top but reverses back down within a few bars, this can function like a wedge top... The first two pushes up are the highs of the double top, and the third push up is the breakout above the double top.
candidates.description: A failed breakout above a double top (price closes back below the double top's level within a few bars of breaking above it) is treated as the third push of a three-push top: short the reversal back below the double top level, expecting at least a scalp and possibly a measured move.
candidates.book_order_type: sell stop one tick below the failed-breakout reversal bar's low

complexity.reason: needs a double-top pivot pair plus a failed-breakout test against that level within a bar-count window

notes: Likely overlaps with a double-top-specific failed-breakout candidate expected from Chapter 8 (double top and bottom pullbacks) and with FailedBreakoutBelowSwingLow (V02-22)'s mirror; dedup pass should compare.

candidates.name: WedgeInTradingRangeTakeFirstSignal
candidates.quote: If there is a wedge reversal in a trading range, it may look and act more like a wedge pullback because there is no trend to reverse. When that is the case, taking the first signal is usually a profitable approach.
candidates.description: When a three-push pattern forms inside a trading range (no established trend to reverse), treat it like a with-trend wedge pullback and take the first reversal signal rather than waiting for a second entry.
candidates.pseudocode:
// research: 'is a trading range' is itself a research-grade concept per MINING.md
takeFirstSignal = isThreePushPattern(direction, pivotStrength) && marketIsInTradingRange;
candidates.book_order_type: n/a (overrides V05-05's wait-for-second-entry rule when no trend is present)

complexity.reason: depends on classifying 'the market is in a trading range', which itself needs a design decision before it can be coded (per MINING.md's own example of a research-grade concept)

candidates.name: WedgeSecondPushMomentumResetsCount
candidates.quote: If, after the pullback from the first push, the market creates an especially strong second push, many traders will reset the count and consider it to be the new first push... The stronger the momentum is on the second push, the more likely it is that the market will have reset the count and the more likely it is that there will be a fourth push.
candidates.description: When the second push of a three-push pattern shows especially strong momentum, expect the count to reset (traders treat it as a new first push), which raises the odds that a fourth push is needed before the reversal signal should be trusted.
candidates.book_order_type: n/a (gates whether to trust the third-push reversal signal or wait for a fourth)

complexity.reason: 'especially strong momentum' for a single leg has no stated bar-level test; needs a design decision (e.g. trend-bar count, average body multiple, or overlap) before coding

candidates.name: OpeningReversalSteepWedgeException
candidates.quote: Wedges are often opening reversal patterns... Although you should never look for a reversal from such a steep, tight wedge after the first hour or two, they can be reliable opening reversal setups.
candidates.description: A very steep, tight three-push wedge is only a reliable reversal setup near the session open; the same steep/tight wedge shape should not be traded as a reversal later in the session (after the first one or two hours).

complexity.reason: combines V05-01's pivot detection with the same undefined 'tight/steep channel' measure as V05-10, plus a session-clock check

notes: 'First hour or two' is the book's own hedge on the exact cutoff; openingWindowMinutes is a reading of that as 120 minutes.

candidates.name: FailedWedgeTradeWithChannelInstead
candidates.quote: If the breakout is weak, traders assume that it will fail and they look for the channel to continue. They will then enter in the direction of the wedge channel and not in the countertrend direction... traders will look to short the low 1 or low 2 that is created by the failed upside breakout.
candidates.description: If the reversal breakout out of a wedge looks weak, skip the countertrend reversal trade and instead fade the failed breakout back in the direction of the original wedge channel (a low-1/low-2 or high-1/high-2 setup created by that failed breakout).
candidates.book_order_type: n/a (redirects the trade toward a with-channel low1/low2 (or high1/high2) setup instead of the countertrend reversal)

complexity.reason: 'weak breakout' has no stated bar-level test; the low1/low2 setup itself is a separate counting primitive expected elsewhere in the corpus

notes: The low1/low2 (high1/high2) counting setup this refers to is a shared primitive expected to already exist (bar-counting chapter of the Ranges book); not redefined here.

candidates.name: FailedWedgeSecondAttemptExpectsProtractedTrend
candidates.quote: Sometimes, just after failing, it reverses back and creates a second attempt at reversing the trend; when this happens, the new trend is usually protracted (lasting at least 10 bars) and it usually has at least two legs.
candidates.description: When a wedge-reversal breakout fails and price quickly reverses back to make a second attempt at the reversal (a breakout pullback from the failed extreme), treat the resulting new trend as likely to be protracted: at least N bars and at least two legs.
candidates.book_order_type: n/a (sets a bars/legs expectation used to size trade management, e.g. how long to hold before trailing)

complexity.reason: needs the same pivot-based wedge/failure detection as V05-03 plus a bar-count window to test whether price reversed back through the extreme

notes: This is a specific instance of the general 'breakout pullback' primitive (Ranges book Ch.5) applied to a failed wedge extreme.

rejected.quote: most trend channel line overshoots have a wedge shape, but it is often so stretched out that it is not worth looking at it.
rejected.reason: pure discretion ('not worth looking at'), no bar-level test given for how stretched out disqualifies a setup

rejected.quote: The reason moves end at targets is that most trades are being done by computers, and their algorithms are based on math and logic.
rejected.reason: market-structure commentary about other participants' order flow, not decidable from this engine's OHLCV/position state

chapter_summary: Chapter 5 generalizes wedges, triangles, expanding triangles, double/triple tops and bottoms, and failed double-top/bottom breakouts into one primitive: three sequential swing pushes in one direction (V05-01), independent of whether the connecting lines converge, run parallel, or diverge. It then splits trading logic into with-trend wedge-flag entries (first signal, V05-04), countertrend wedge-reversal entries (wait for a second signal unless exceptional, V05-05), duration heuristics (10-20 bars for flags, 20+ for reversals, V05-06/07), a parabolic-acceleration climax classifier (V05-08), a shrinking-stairs momentum-fade classifier (V05-09), a repeatedly-invoked but never-quantified 'tight channel' avoidance rule (V05-10, kept research-grade), a micro-wedge variant at minimal pivot strength (V05-11), a fine-grained one-to-two-tick minor-breakout continuation pattern that deliberately trades WITH the breakout rather than against it (V05-12), a failed-double-top-breakout-as-wedge-top variant (V05-13), a trading-range exception to the second-entry rule (V05-14, research-grade since 'trading range' itself is undefined), a momentum-driven count-reset heuristic (V05-15, research-grade), an opening-only exception for otherwise-untradeable steep wedges (V05-16), a redirect-to-the-channel rule for weak reversal breakouts (V05-17), and a failed-wedge-then-second-attempt expectation of a protracted >=10-bar, >=2-leg trend (V05-18). Several candidates (V05-04, V05-06, V05-07) are near-verbatim restatements of Ranges-book Chapter 18 primitives (R18-02/04/05), which this chapter itself cross-references. The remainder of the chapter (Figures 5.1-5.12) is worked chart examples with bar numbers; the general rules above were extracted from the surrounding prose, not the specific bar annotations.
